title: Context and threads: flowOn, the invariant, and channelFlow
goal: By the end you can explain why emit may not change context, say exactly what flowOn builds and which part of a chain it moves, predict the threads of a chain with several flowOn calls, and fan in several producers with channelFlow.
opening:
The grocer's van has been. With the shopping comes a delivery note, one line per item, such as `flour,2000,g`, read by the old reader from Flow basics whose `readLine` holds its thread while it waits. Each line means an item to put away and write in the pantry book. Only one person may write in that book at a time, and it lives at the kitchen table. The reading is slow, waiting work, and it belongs in the back room, on another thread.

One line moves it: `flowOn(io)`. The reading goes to the back room, the pantry book stays at the table, and the print order changes in a way that surprises people. The obvious alternative, wrapping the read and the `emit` in `withContext(io)`, is the one the inspector refused in Inside flow { }.

In this lesson, we'll watch `flowOn` let the reader run ahead, build it by hand from a channel, count the rooms when a chain has several walls, and let several cooks share one hatch with `channelFlow`. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A flow reads three lines of a delivery note at once and emits each item. The collector needs 30 ms to put each item away. You add `.flowOn(io)` before `collect`. What is the order of the `read` and `stored` lines now?
options: read 1, stored 1, read 2, stored 2, read 3, stored 3, the same as without flowOn
read 1, read 2, read 3, then stored 1, stored 2, stored 3
stored 1, stored 2, stored 3, then the reads
The flow throws "Flow invariant is violated"
warmup.why: With a different dispatcher, `flowOn` runs the reader in a second coroutine and puts a 64-slot channel between the two sides. The reader's `emit` now only puts the item into the channel, so it reads all three lines before the first 30 ms of putting away is done. The invariant error is for `withContext` around `emit`, not for `flowOn`.

sections.h: Add flowOn and the reader runs ahead of the collector
sections.body:
Here is the delivery note as a flow. A **dispatcher** is the part of the coroutines library that decides which thread runs a coroutine. `flowOn(io)` asks for the code above it to run on `io`, here a dispatcher with one thread named `io-thread`. Putting an item away takes the collector 30 ms. Predict the order of the six lines:

```kotlin
deliveryItems()                      // prints "read <item> on <thread>", then emits the item
    .flowOn(io)
    .collect { item ->
        delay(30)                    // put it away and write it in the pantry book
        println("stored  $item on ${Thread.currentThread().name}")
    }
```

```java
// Java equivalent: a reader thread puts items into a 64-slot BlockingQueue,
// and the main thread takes them out and stores them
BlockingQueue<String> hatch = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64);
new Thread(() -> { for (String item : items) put(hatch, item); put(hatch, END); }, "io-thread").start();
for (String item = hatch.take(); !item.equals(END); item = hatch.take()) {
    Thread.sleep(30);                // put it away and write it in the pantry book
    System.out.println("stored  " + item + " on " + Thread.currentThread().getName());
}
```

Without `flowOn` you get lesson 1's pattern: read, stored, read, stored, all on `main`. With it:

```text
read    flour  on io-thread
read    eggs   on io-thread
read    milk   on io-thread
stored  flour  on main
stored  eggs   on main
stored  milk   on main
```

The reader ran ahead. It read all three lines before the first item was put away, so its `emit` calls returned without waiting for the collector. In lesson 1, `emit` couldn't return before the collector did. Something now sits between the two sides and holds values, and the two sides run on different threads. The Java twin prints the same six lines, and it shows what that something is: a queue.

Why not just wrap the read and the `emit` in `withContext(io)`? `withContext` runs one block of code in another context and comes back, as Dispatchers and the coroutine context showed. Lesson 2 showed what `flow { }` says to it here: "Flow invariant is violated". It also showed why. A hand-written raw `Flow` with no inspector ran its collector on `DefaultDispatcher-worker-1`. The collector runs inside `emit`, so an `emit` on an IO thread drags the collector onto that thread too.

That's a real bug, not a matter of style. The pantry book is not **thread-safe**: two threads writing in it at the same moment can mix up their lines, so all the writing must happen on one side. To move the reader and leave the collector alone, you have to break the call chain between them. That takes a second coroutine and a place to keep values in between, and we can build both from tools the coroutines track already gave us.

steps: Read `FlowOnOrder.kt`. It runs the delivery note twice, without and with `.flowOn(io)`. Write down both orders before you run it.
Run it.
Replace `.flowOn(io)` with `.flowOn(CoroutineName("reader"))` (import `kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineName`). Predict the order and the threads, then run it.
Run the Java twin, `FlowOnOrderJava`.

code.title: FlowOnOrder.kt
code.src:
package workbench.flows.l03

import kotlinx.coroutines.asCoroutineDispatcher
import kotlinx.coroutines.delay
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flowOn
import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking
import java.util.concurrent.Executors

val deliveryNote = listOf("flour,2000,g", "eggs,12,pcs", "milk,1000,ml")

/** Reads the grocer's delivery note. Each line is read at once; it prints which thread read it. */
fun deliveryItems(): Flow<String> = flow {
    for (line in deliveryNote) {
        val item = line.substringBefore(",")
        println("read    %-6s on %s".format(item, Thread.currentThread().name))
        emit(item)
    }
}

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val io = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor { r -> Thread(r, "io-thread") }.asCoroutineDispatcher()

    println("=== plain, as in lesson 1")
    deliveryItems().collect { item ->
        delay(30)                                   // put it away and write it in the pantry book
        println("stored  %-6s on %s".format(item, Thread.currentThread().name))
    }

    println("=== with .flowOn(io)")
    deliveryItems().flowOn(io).collect { item ->
        delay(30)
        println("stored  %-6s on %s".format(item, Thread.currentThread().name))
    }
    io.close()
}

sections.h: Several flowOn calls: two walls, three rooms, read from the bottom up
sections.body:
`flowOn` changes the context of the operators above it, up to the previous `flowOn`, and nothing below it. With two of them you get two walls and three rooms:

```kotlin
flow { for (i in 1..2) { log("emit", i); emit(i) } }
    .map { log("map1", it); it }
    .flowOn(io)                                // wall 1: everything above runs on io
    .map { log("map2", it); it }
    .flowOn(cpu)                               // wall 2: map2 runs on cpu
    .collect { log("collect", it) }            // the collector's room: main
```

```java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: subscribeOn moves the source, publishOn moves what follows,
// and toStream() hands values back to the calling thread through a queue
Flux.range(1, 2)
    .doOnNext(i -> log("emit", i))
    .map(i -> { log("map1", i); return i; })
    .subscribeOn(io)
    .publishOn(cpu)
    .map(i -> { log("map2", i); return i; })
    .toStream()
    .forEach(i -> log("collect", i));
```

Coroutine debug mode, a JVM setting (`kotlinx.coroutines.debug`) that adds each coroutine's number to its thread's name, counts the coroutines for you:

```text
  emit     1   thread=io-thread @coroutine#3
  map1     1   thread=io-thread @coroutine#3
  emit     2   thread=io-thread @coroutine#3
  map1     2   thread=io-thread @coroutine#3
  map2     1   thread=cpu-thread @coroutine#2
  collect  1   thread=main @coroutine#1
  map2     2   thread=cpu-thread @coroutine#2
  collect  2   thread=main @coroutine#1
```

Three coroutines, so two channels. The order of lines across threads can change from run to run, but each stage always stays in its room.

Notice the direction. Reactor's `publishOn` moves what comes after it. Kotlin's `flowOn` moves what comes before it: it only ever looks up. If you think in Reactor, read `flowOn` from the bottom up.

Three variants surprise people. First, two `flowOn` calls with nothing between them fuse into one wall, and the first one, nearest the source, wins. The `toString()` of `flowOf(1, 2, 3).flowOn(Dispatchers.IO).flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)` ends with `ChannelFlowOperatorImpl[context=Dispatchers.IO]`. (That string is a debug aid, not an API.) A `map` between them stops the fusion. Second, `flowOn(CoroutineName("renamed"))` keeps the dispatcher, so it builds no wall; it only puts a new name on the same room. The lines alternate on `main` like a plain flow, and the upstream's lines show `main @renamed#1`: the collector's coroutine number with a new name on it. Third, a `Job` in `flowOn` is refused as soon as you build the operator, with "Flow context cannot contain job in it."

The common slip comes from looking down instead of up. Someone puts `flowOn` at the end of a chain and expects it to cover only the slow part:

```kotlin
readLines(reader)
    .map { parseDeliveryLine(it) }
    .onEach { pantry.store(it) }     // above flowOn, so this runs on io as well
    .flowOn(io)
    .collect()
```

```java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: subscribeOn moves the source, and with no publishOn the stores run on io too
readLines(reader)
    .map(DeliveryLine::parse)
    .doOnNext(pantry::store)         // runs on the io scheduler too
    .subscribeOn(io)
    .blockLast();
```

Here the pantry writes end up behind the wall, on `io`, which is exactly where the pantry book must never go. Put `flowOn` directly below the last line that must move: `.map { parseDeliveryLine(it) }.flowOn(io).onEach { pantry.store(it) }`. That one-line move is the first half of this lesson's lab.

`flowOn` never moves the collector, wherever you put it. If the collecting side blocks, wrap the terminal call instead, `withContext(io) { flow.collect { ... } }`, as Flow basics showed.

**Read `flowOn` from the bottom up. It moves what's above it, up to the previous `flowOn`.**

Every room so far had one cook, emitting one plate at a time. Tonight two cooks share the kitchen, and the diner wants plates from both.

compare.title: flowOn by hand: a channel in Kotlin, a BlockingQueue in Java

java.title: HandMadeFlowOnJava.java (abridged)

kotlin.title: HandMadeFlowOn.kt (abridged)

compare.note: Both versions have the same three parts: a second worker, a 64-slot hatch, and a loop on the caller's side that empties it. Three things differ, and all of them matter in real programs. A full `BlockingQueue` blocks a thread, while a full channel suspends a coroutine. A queue can't be closed, so the Java version needs an end marker, while `produce` closes its channel when its block ends. And the Kotlin version stops cleanly: if the collector fails or stops early, `coroutineScope` cancels the `produce` coroutine. In the Java version the reader thread keeps running, blocked on a full queue, until someone interrupts it.

worked.title: Make the delivery import testable in virtual time

steps.say: Say the grocer's website lets the reader fetch only one line per second, so the reader waits before each read. The first version hard-codes the dispatcher. A test with `runTest` looks fine, but it is slow, and its virtual clock says nothing happened. In a run with three lines on a busy machine, `TestTime.kt` printed `virtual=0 ms, wall=3533 ms`: `Dispatchers.Default` lives outside the test's scheduler, so its `delay` calls are real.
Inject the dispatcher instead. The real program passes `Dispatchers.IO`, a test passes something else. Give it a default so callers don't have to care.

For timing tests, pass a test dispatcher that shares the test's scheduler. Its `delay` calls move the virtual clock, so the same three lines run in milliseconds and the clock reads exactly 3000. `flowOn` still builds its channel, because a second `StandardTestDispatcher` is a different dispatcher object.

For "which side ran where" tests, pass a real executor with one named thread, and record thread names in the fakes. That is how the lab's test checks that `readLine` ran on `test-io` and `pantry.store` on the test thread. Strip the ` @coroutine#N` suffix that debug mode adds when tests run with `-ea`.

steps: Run the tests. Three of the five fail. Read the messages: one lists the threads that called `pantry.store`, and two quote "Emission from another coroutine is detected".
Fix `importDelivery` by moving one line. Reading and parsing must run on `io`; storing and the collector must not.

hints: `flowOn` moves the operators above it, up to the previous `flowOn`. Ask which lines must run on `io`, and put `flowOn` directly below the last of them.
Inside `channelFlow { }`, `this` is a `ProducerScope`: a `CoroutineScope` you can `launch` in and a `SendChannel` you can `send` to. You don't need `awaitClose`; that's for `callbackFlow`.
You don't need to close the channel or join the children. `channelFlow` completes by itself when its block and all its children are done.

The test cooks use `delay`. `runTest`'s virtual clock covers them, because `channelFlow`'s children inherit the test dispatcher. The merged flow should complete at 390 ms of virtual time, the slower cook's last plate.

Then answer without running it: where does the block of `flow { }` run, where does your `emit` run, and how many emits can return while the collector holds the first value?

recap: The collector runs inside `emit`, so `emit` must run in the collector's context. `withContext` around `emit` would drag the collector onto another thread, and `flow { }` refuses it.
When the dispatcher changes, `flowOn` runs the upstream in a second coroutine and puts a channel between the two halves, 64 slots by default: a wall with a hatch. The producer can get 65 emits ahead.

`flowOn` moves only the operators above it, up to the previous `flowOn`. Two calls make two walls and three rooms; two adjacent calls fuse, and the first one wins. With the same dispatcher, as in `flowOn(CoroutineName(...))`, there is no channel.
To emit from several coroutines, use `channelFlow`: `send` is safe from any child, and the flow completes after every child. `produceIn` hands you the channel itself, hot, in your scope.
In tests, inject the dispatcher that `flowOn` uses. `flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)` inside `runTest` runs on the real clock.
The limit: every hatch here had the default 64 spots and made the producer wait when full. Choosing the size, and what to drop instead of waiting, is the next lesson.
closing:
We started with a delivery note to read in the back room and a pantry book that must stay at the table. `flowOn` builds the wall: the code above it runs in a second coroutine, a hatch with 64 spots sits between, and the collector never moves. Several walls make several rooms, and `channelFlow` lets several cooks share one hatch.

Now find each `flowOn` in your own code and read its chain from the bottom up. Check that nothing which must stay put, such as a client that isn't thread-safe, sits above it.

Next, we'll look at the shelf in the hatch. How many plates should it hold, and which plate is lost when it's full?

quiz.q: `flow { emit(1) }.map { a(it) }.flowOn(io).map { b(it) }.collect { c(it) }`. Where do `a`, `b` and `c` run?
options: All three on io
`a` on io; `b` and `c` in the collector's context
`a` and `b` on io; `c` in the collector's context
`a` in the collector's context; `b` and `c` on io
quiz.why: `flowOn` moves what is above it, up to the previous `flowOn`, and nothing below it. The tempting answer "`a` and `b` on io" reads `flowOn` like Reactor's `publishOn`, which moves what follows it.

quiz.q: A collector holds the first value and doesn't return. The upstream is `flow { repeat(200) { emit(it) } }.flowOn(io)`. How many `emit` calls return meanwhile?
quiz.why: `flowOn` with a new dispatcher puts a `Channel.BUFFERED` channel in between: 64 slots. The producer fills all 64, and one more value is already in the collector's hands, so 65 emits have returned. A plain flow gives 0.

options: Dispatchers.IO: adjacent flowOn calls fuse, and the first one wins
Dispatchers.Default: the last flowOn wins
Both, one after the other, through two channels
Neither: the two calls cancel out and it runs on the collector's thread
quiz.why: Adjacent `flowOn` calls fuse into one, and the context of the first one, nearest the source, takes precedence for each key. `toString()` shows `ChannelFlowOperatorImpl[context=Dispatchers.IO]`. A `map` between them would stop the fusion and give two walls.

quiz.q: You have two flows of plates, `grill` and `oven`, and want one flow that delivers both as they are ready, without waiting for one cook to finish first. Which builder fits?
options: `flow { coroutineScope { launch { grill.collect { emit(it) } }; launch { oven.collect { emit(it) } } } }`
`flow { withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { grill.collect { emit(it) } } }`
`channelFlow { launch { grill.collect { send(it) } }; launch { oven.collect { send(it) } } }`
`flow { grill.collect { emit(it) }; oven.collect { emit(it) } }`
quiz.why: `channelFlow` gives each child a `send` that is safe from any coroutine, and completes after both. The `flow { }` with `launch` fails with "Emission from another coroutine is detected". The last option is legal but sequential: the oven's plates start only after the grill is done.

quiz.q: From lesson 2: `flow { coroutineScope { emit(1) } }` passes the context check, but `flow { coroutineScope { launch { emit(1) } } }` fails. Why the second one?
options: `launch` always switches to another dispatcher
The emitting Job is a launched child, not a scope, so two coroutines could emit at once into a collector that isn't thread-safe
`coroutineScope` is not allowed inside `flow { }`
`launch` runs after the flow has already completed
quiz.why: The check allows a different `Job` only if it reaches the collector's `Job` through scope coroutines such as `coroutineScope`. A `launch`ed child could run at the same time as another, so the inspector refuses its emits and points you to `channelFlow`. `launch` keeps the parent's dispatcher unless you pass one.

flashcards.back: The collector runs inside `emit`, so it would run on an IO thread it never asked for. Use `flowOn` on the upstream instead.

flashcards.front: What does `flowOn(io)` build when `io` differs from the collector's dispatcher?
flashcards.back: A second coroutine that runs the upstream on `io` and sends into a channel (64 slots by default), plus a loop that emits each value in the collector's coroutine.

flashcards.front: Which part of a chain does `flowOn` move?
flashcards.back: Only the operators above it, up to the previous `flowOn`. The collector never moves.
No. The dispatcher is unchanged, so the upstream runs inline with the new name.

flashcards.front: `.flowOn(A).flowOn(B)` with nothing between them: which dispatcher runs the upstream?
flashcards.back: A. Adjacent `flowOn` calls fuse into one, and the first one (nearest the source) wins for each context key.
When its block and every coroutine launched inside it have finished. The block itself may return much earlier.

flashcards.front: Why inject the dispatcher you pass to `flowOn`?
flashcards.back: `flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)` inside `runTest` runs on the real clock: three 1 s delays took about 3.5 s of wall time and 0 ms of virtual time.

terms.plain: An operator that runs the part of the flow above it in another context, through a channel when the dispatcher changes.
A queue between coroutines: `send` suspends when it is full, `receive` suspends when it is empty. In the kitchen, the hatch with its shelf.
The internal base class behind `flowOn`, `buffer`, `channelFlow` and `produceIn`: a flow that can run its upstream in a second coroutine and empty a channel.
Adjacent channel-based operators merging into one channel with one combined configuration.
A builder whose block can launch coroutines that all `send` into one channel. It completes after all of them.
Launches a coroutine in your scope that collects a flow, and returns its channel: a hot stream you must consume or cancel.
The receiver of `channelFlow`'s block: a `CoroutineScope` and a `SendChannel` in one.

explain_back.prompt: A friend moved a blocking delivery-note reader with `withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { emit(line) }`, got "Flow invariant is violated", and asks why Kotlin forbids something so obvious. Explain it, and say what `flowOn` does instead.
explain_back.answer: In a flow, emit isn't a hand-off. It's a direct call into the collector, so the collector's code runs inside emit. If emit ran inside withContext(Dispatchers.IO), our collector, the part that writes in the pantry book, would suddenly run on an IO thread it never asked for, next to code that isn't thread-safe. flow { } checks every emit and refuses that. flowOn solves it by breaking the call chain. When the dispatcher changes, it starts a second coroutine on IO that runs everything above flowOn and sends each value into a channel with 64 slots, and on our side a loop takes values out and calls our collector in its own coroutine. So the reader runs on IO, can get up to 65 values ahead, and the collector stays exactly where it was. It only moves what's above it, so we put it right under the blocking read.

deeper.body:
Some details of `flowOn` only show up in real programs.

It can lose values in flight on cancellation. Its KDoc says that "flows operating across different dispatchers might lose some in-flight elements when cancelled", and that the operator "ensures that downstream flow does not resume on cancellation even if the element was already emitted by the upstream flow". For the delivery import that means the reader may have read lines that never reached the pantry book. If that matters, track what was stored, not what was read.

Whether a channel appears depends on dispatcher objects, not threads. With a collector already on `Dispatchers.IO`, `flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)` stays sequential, with no channel. With a collector on `Dispatchers.Default`, `flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)` creates one, even though the two dispatchers share threads, because they are different objects.

Stability in 1.11.0: `flowOn`, `channelFlow`, `callbackFlow` and `produceIn` compile with no opt-in. `CoroutineScope.produce`, which the hand-built `myFlowOn` uses, is `@ExperimentalCoroutinesApi`. Use the library's operators in real code and keep `myFlowOn` as the model in your head.

`callbackFlow`, from lesson 9 of the coroutines track, is a subclass of the same `channelFlow` builder. The difference is one check: if its block returns while the channel is still open, it throws an `IllegalStateException` telling you to call `awaitClose { ... }` at the end. Lesson 8 of this track wraps a listener API with it.

`buffer()` is the same machine as `flowOn` without the context change, and neighbouring channel operators fuse into one channel. Lesson 4 of this track takes that apart, using `toString()` as a peek under the hood.
